extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in political philosophy, civil liberty, and the proper scope of social authority (philosophers, legislators, educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for when society may legitimately interfere with an individual's conduct — distinguishing self-regarding acts from acts affecting others, and prescribing appropriate forms of social response (law, opinion, persuasion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain allocation between individuality and society
rubrics_metrics.description: To individuality should belong the part of life in which it is chiefly the individual that is interested; to society, the part which chiefly interests society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each will receive its proper share if each has that which more particularly concerns it. Use this as the basic rule for deciding whether an area of conduct falls under individual sovereignty or social jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of injury to others as ground for enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is justified in enforcing conduct which consists first in not injuring the interests of one another; or rather certain interests ... ought to be considered as rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an act infringes others' rights or harms their interests, society may lawfully intervene and compel compliance; such prevention of harm is a central justification for legal coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to bear share of social burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person's bearing his share (to be fixed on some equitable principle) of the labours and sacrifices incurred for defending the society or its members from injury and molestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may enforce duties that secure collective defence and protection (e.g., contributions, service), and can do so 'at all costs' against those who refuse to fulfil them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social punishment by opinion versus legal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts of an individual may be hurtful to others, or wanting in due consideration for their welfare, without going the length of violating any of their constituted rights. The offender may then be justly punished by opinion though not by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conduct is harmful but does not breach legal rights, non-legal sanctions (public disapproval, ostracism) may be appropriate; whether to move from censure to legal sanction depends on whether interference would promote the general welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regarding actions should be free from social and legal interference
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no room for entertaining any such question when a person's conduct affects the interests of no persons besides himself ... In all such cases there should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions that affect only the agent (and competent others consenting) are protected: neither law nor social compulsion ought to override the individual's choice in purely self-regarding matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use persuasion and education, not coercion, for self-regarding matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence can find other instruments to persuade people to their good, than whips and scourges ... the self-regarding virtues should be inculcated by conviction and persuasion as well as by compulsion during education; after education, persuasion rather than coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social efforts to improve individuals' private conduct should rely on education, example and argument; compulsion is appropriate only for preventing clear harm to others or fulfilling communal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to the individual's superior knowledge of his own circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: He himself is the final judge. The most ordinary man or woman has means of knowledge immeasurably surpassing those that can be possessed by any one else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because persons are best placed to judge their own feelings and circumstances, general presumptions used to override individual judgment risk being wrong or misapplied; this argues for restraint in social interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of general rules for interpersonal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: In the conduct of human beings towards one another, it is necessary that general rules should for the most part be observed, in order that people may know what they have to expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between persons, predictable general rules are required for social order; the need for such rules can justify some limitation on individuality where others' expectations and rights are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of individuality and diversity for human development
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not by wearing down into uniformity all that is individual in themselves, but by cultivating it and calling it forth ... that human beings become a noble and beautiful object of contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should promote and protect diverse modes of life and tastes, because individuality enriches human life and is instrumental to progress and the flourishing of the whole community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of genius and eccentricity as social goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius can only breathe freely in an atmosphere of freedom ... the mere example of nonconformity, the mere refusal to bend the knee to custom, is itself a service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional individuals and eccentricity should be tolerated and even encouraged as they initiate improvements and correct the tyranny of mediocrity; stifling them impoverishes society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression permissible only to prevent encroachment on others' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: As much compression as is necessary to prevent the stronger specimens of human nature from encroaching on the rights of others, cannot be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints on individuality are legitimate only to the extent needed to stop interference with others' liberties; beyond that, compression is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about the despotism of custom and enforced uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The despotism of custom is everywhere the standing hindrance to human advancement ... The spirit of improvement is antagonistic to the sway of Custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymaking and social norms should beware of enforcing sameness for its own sake; freedom and variety of situations are necessary conditions for progress and must be preserved against conformist pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against basing interference on general presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The interference of society to overrule his judgment and purposes in what only regards himself, must be grounded on general presumptions; which may be altogether wrong, and even if right, are as likely as not to be misapplied to individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because social judgments are fallible and may misread particulars, they should not be used lightly to justify coercion in personal matters; individualized circumstances require deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of social sentiment (admiration, contempt) without legal coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not mean that the feelings with which a person is regarded by others, ought not to be in any way affected by his self-regarding qualities or deficiencies ... a sentiment the opposite of admiration will follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social reactions (admiration, distaste, contempt) to private character are natural and permissible forms of social evaluation, but they do not by themselves justify legal punishment or removal of liberty.
